executive_summary: NZD/USD closed the gated weekday store at 0.59164 on 31 August 2026, with the RBNZ Trade-Weighted Index at 66.71 on 1 September, and the currency has gone almost nowhere against the dollar for a year: +0.48 per cent over one month, +0.98 per cent over three, +0.25 per cent over six and -1.04 per cent over twelve. That stasis conceals a violent crosscurrent. New Zealand is the G10 outlier on inflation, with headline CPI at 4.1 per cent year on year in the June 2026 quarter, the highest since the fourth quarter of 2023, and the Reserve Bank has already turned, raising the Official Cash Rate 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent on 8 July 2026 with a further 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent priced at a 94 per cent probability into the 2 September Monetary Policy Statement. Yet the overshoot is almost entirely imported - tradables inflation is 4.9 per cent on a 27.5 per cent petrol contribution while the Reserve Bank's own preferred sectoral factor model core has been pinned at 2.7 per cent for four consecutive quarters, inside the 1 to 3 per cent band - and one-year inflation expectations collapsed 81 basis points to 2.60 per cent in the August survey. On valuation the BIS real effective exchange rate of 101.12 for the June 2026 period sits almost exactly on its own index base after falling 3.74 points over the year, which leaves the New Zealand dollar modestly cheap on a relative basis against a US dollar at 107.84, a sterling at 111.41 and above all an Australian dollar at 115.92, and the resulting 12.8 per cent REER gap to the Australian dollar is the single largest relative-value fact in this report. The central tension is that a central bank is being forced to tighten into a domestic economy that is visibly cracking: unemployment at 5.6 per cent is a decade high, private-sector wages are growing 2.0 per cent against 4.1 per cent inflation, retail volumes fell 0.5 per cent in the June quarter for the first time in two years, and house prices are 0.7 per cent lower over the year and roughly 17 per cent below their November 2021 peak. We are tactically Bullish at conviction 3 on the hawkish track revision and a leveraged-fund short of 31,994 contracts, and strategically Bearish at conviction 2 as the fuel base effect reverses, the terms of trade deteriorate and the Federal Reserve is itself priced for a hike rather than a cut - with the explicit caveat that a September track pointing at a 3.5 per cent terminal rate would hold the tactical case open considerably longer than we expect.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: The RBNZ Trade-Weighted Index at 66.71 on 1 September sits 0.11 points above the 66.6 level the Reserve Bank assumed in its May 2026 projections and 0.64 points below the 67.35 peak struck on 24 August. That is a currency doing almost exactly what the central bank forecast it would do, which removes the exchange rate as an independent source of policy surprise in September, but the July Record of Meeting explicitly warned that a sustained lower exchange rate would add to medium-term inflation pressure - meaning the Bank has told the market it will lean against TWI weakness but has said nothing about leaning against strength.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: At 101.12 on the BIS real effective measure the market is pricing the New Zealand dollar as an ordinary developed-market currency with no particular carry appeal and no particular distress, which is a reasonable reading of a 2.50 per cent policy rate sitting seventh of ten in the G10 and a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP. What the level does not price is the 12.77 per cent relative gap that has opened against the Australian dollar in eighteen months, nor the possibility that the Reserve Bank publishes a terminal rate of around 3.5 per cent on 2 September against market pricing of roughly one further move beyond that meeting. The cheapness is real but it is cheapness against the Antipodean peer rather than against the dollar.
valuation.actionability: The valuation signal is structural rather than tactical: a 6.23 per cent REER-relative discount to the US dollar will not close inside four weeks and has not closed in twelve months of trying. It is directly actionable only in the AUD/NZD cross, where the 12.77 per cent relative REER gap, a 1.21137 spot at the 86th percentile of its 52-week range and a 4.53 per cent realised volatility combine into the highest information-per-unit-of-risk expression in the New Zealand dollar complex.

That is a textbook divergence: fast money is pressing a short into an event while real money has already stepped out of the way. The currency brief sets the notable threshold for this market at plus or minus 30,000 contracts, so the leveraged short is marginally past the level at which squeezes historically become disorderly.
positioning_summary.contrarian_assessment: A leveraged short of 31,994 contracts running into a Monetary Policy Statement with a 94 per cent priced hike and a brand new published OCR track is the most asymmetric configuration in the dossier, because the decision itself cannot disappoint the shorts but the track can. Against that, the same figures are subject to a genuine and unresolved data conflict - the legacy non-commercial series carried in the pipeline calendar shows minus 14,200 for the same report date and a large positive weekly swing, disagreeing with the Traders in Financial Futures series on both level and direction - and we have lowered positioning confidence to 50 tactically and 45 strategically as a result. The squeeze case is real but it rests on a number we cannot independently reconcile.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime is one of conspicuous non-response. Over twelve months the New Zealand dollar has fallen 1.04 per cent against a US dollar whose broad index dropped 2.04 points in August alone, while the VIX collapsed 6.23 points to 14.43, high-yield spreads tightened to 263 basis points and the S&P 500 closed August at 7,686.14 - a combination that should have lifted the highest-beta risk currency in the G10 and did not. What the currency has done instead is lose 8.0 per cent to the Australian dollar over the year and 6.1 per cent to the Norwegian krone, which identifies the driver precisely: this is a relative-rates story, not a risk story, and New Zealand is on the wrong side of it with a 2.50 per cent policy rate against 4.35 in Australia and 4.25 in Norway. The dominant narrative going into September is whether a central bank that hiked in July off the back of a 4.1 per cent headline print will publish a track that ratifies the market's roughly one further move or one that points at 3.5 per cent. Volatility is low, positioning is short, dairy has printed four consecutive positive auctions after a 4.9 per cent collapse in early July, and nothing is trending.

sovereign_yields.curve_shape: Steeply positive. New Zealand runs the steepest major curve in the G10 by a wide margin. The orthodox reading of a steep curve as a growth signal is wrong here: this curve is steep because the front end is anchored by an OCR of 2.50 per cent that the market expects to rise only slowly, while the long end carries the term premium of a small, twin-deficit borrower with two of three rating agencies on negative outlook. A hawkish September track flattens this curve from the front, and that flattening is the cleanest confirmation signal for the tactical view.

tactical.analysis: The Official Cash Rate is 2.50 per cent after a 25 basis point increase on 8 July 2026, the Reserve Bank's first hike since May 2023, and the market prices a 94 per cent probability of a further 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent at the 2 September Monetary Policy Statement. That places New Zealand seventh of ten on policy rate in the G10, 112.5 basis points below the Federal Reserve midpoint of 3.625 per cent, 185 basis points below the Reserve Bank of Australia at 4.35 per cent, 175 below Norges Bank and 125 below the Bank of England, while earning 250 basis points over the Swiss National Bank, 150 over the Bank of Japan and 25 over both the ECB and the Bank of Canada. The decision itself is not the catalyst - at 94 per cent priced it cannot surprise on the upside - but the republished OCR track is, because the May 2026 track is the only one in existence and it predates both the July hike and the 4.1 per cent CPI print. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the direction of the New Zealand policy differential improves while its level remains unattractive, and that distinction sets both the stance and the modest confidence. The Reserve Bank is one of only two G10 central banks in an active tightening cycle, and even the conservative May track lifts the OCR to a 3.1 per cent quarterly average by mid-2027 from 2.50 per cent today, which mechanically narrows the gap to the Reserve Bank of Australia from 185 basis points toward 125 and to the Federal Reserve from 112.5 toward 50 if the Federal Reserve stands still. If the Federal Reserve hikes once and the Reserve Bank hikes twice, the differential narrows only 25 basis points over the horizon and NZD/USD carry remains materially negative at roughly minus 87 basis points. The carry the New Zealand dollar does earn is concentrated in legs that are structurally capped or shrinking: 250 basis points over a Swiss National Bank pinned at zero, where no further widening is possible, and 150 over a Bank of Japan with live normalisation risk and Japanese core at 1.8 per cent. Against the Antipodean peer the case is stronger, because the entire 185 basis point gap has to close through New Zealand hiking rather than Australia cutting, and the NZ-AU two-year at roughly minus 121 basis points has already widened roughly 36 basis points against the New Zealand dollar since the July report when it stood at minus 85. The structural drag is the term premium: New Zealand yields 104 basis points more than Canada at ten years on the cached monthly basis against a 25 basis point policy differential, which is the compensation demanded of a small twin-deficit borrower with two of three rating agencies on negative outlook. The honest strategic conclusion is a mild positive on direction with a low ceiling on magnitude. carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is not currently working for the New Zealand dollar and has not worked for a year. The currency earns positive carry against only four of nine G10 peers with policy rates, and against the two peers with the largest negative differentials - the Australian dollar at minus 185 basis points and the Norwegian krone at minus 175 - it has lost 8.0 per cent and 6.1 per cent respectively over twelve months, which is close to what pure carry accrual would predict. The one place carry has worked is NZD/JPY, up 7.49 per cent. The regime is therefore best described as carry-differentiated rather than carry-driven: the New Zealand dollar is a carry funder against the higher-yielding commodity block and a carry recipient only against the zero-rate bloc, which is the opposite of the currency's historical character described in the currency brief and is itself the regime break worth flagging.
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Thin. Against the dollar the carry runs the other way: a long NZD/USD position pays roughly 9.4 basis points a month, about 5.5 pips on a spot of 0.59164, so spot must rise 5.5 pips a month simply to break even, against an ATR14 of 42 pips. Carry provides no meaningful cushion at either horizon and the position must be justified on spot direction alone.

tactical.analysis: Headline CPI rose 1.5 per cent in the June 2026 quarter to 4.1 per cent year on year, the highest annual rate since the fourth quarter of 2023 and up from 3.1 per cent in March, which is what forced the Reserve Bank to hike on 8 July and what makes a second hike a 94 per cent proposition. Over the tactical horizon the data flow supports that: the ANZ Business Outlook for August, released on 31 August, showed pricing intentions up 3.8 points to a net 51.0, cost expectations up to 80.8, one-year inflation expectations up to 3.26 per cent and - the most important cell - activity versus a year ago jumping 6.7 points to 16.4, led by services, which is hard confirmation rather than sentiment. The BusinessNZ manufacturing index at 54.3 in July sits comfortably above its long-run average of 52.5 with production at 57.3, the services index at 50.6 has been above 50 for two consecutive months with activity and sales above 50 for the first time in six, and the composite maps to roughly 2 per cent annual GDP growth against an actual latest print of 0.8 per cent. GDP itself rose 0.8 per cent in the March 2026 quarter, the strongest in nearly three years, with manufacturing up 1.9 per cent. The counterweight is that the inflation is imported, not domestic: tradables inflation jumped to 4.9 per cent from 2.5 while non-tradables eased to 3.4 from 3.5, petrol contributed 23.5 per cent of the annual rise at plus 27.5 per cent, electricity another 8.4 per cent, and the Reserve Bank's preferred sectoral factor model has been pinned at 2.7 per cent for four straight quarters, inside the target band. That composition is why we hold confidence at 53 rather than higher: the level of inflation drives the near-term policy reaction and therefore the currency, but nothing in the composition suggests the Reserve Bank is behind the curve on domestic prices. For the next two to four weeks the binding data points are second-quarter GDP on 17 September and the terms of trade on 3 September, and the survey evidence tilts the GDP risk to the upside of the 0.8 per cent run rate. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the composition of New Zealand inflation matters far more than its level, and the composition is unambiguously disinflationary. The entire overshoot is a fuel and energy shock - tradables at 4.9 per cent against non-tradables at 3.4 and falling - and Brent crude has already fallen 12.07 dollars, or roughly 12 per cent, from 100.31 on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August, which mechanically removes the base effect that produced the 4.1 per cent print. The Reserve Bank's own May track has CPI peaking at 4.3 per cent in the September 2026 quarter and falling to 2.4 per cent by mid-2027 and 2.0 per cent by September 2027, and the July Monetary Policy Review had already revised the near-term peak down to 3.3 per cent for the September quarter. The public has drawn the same conclusion faster than the market: one-year inflation expectations in the August Survey of Expectations collapsed 81 basis points to 2.60 per cent and two-year expectations fell 19 basis points to 2.34 per cent, both comfortably inside the band, which is the single strongest argument that this is not an expectations-driven episode and therefore not persistent. Underneath it the real economy is deteriorating in the ways that matter for medium-term price pressure. Unemployment at 5.6 per cent is the highest since September 2015; the labour cost index for private-sector ordinary time is running at 2.0 per cent against 4.1 per cent inflation, so real wages are falling 2.1 per cent and there is no wage-price mechanism; retail volumes fell 0.5 per cent in the June quarter, the first decline since the September 2024 quarter and the end of six consecutive quarters of growth; house prices are 0.7 per cent lower over the year and roughly 17 per cent below the November 2021 peak in a country where housing is the dominant transmission channel; and services employment has been below 50 for thirty-two consecutive months. The survey-versus-hard-data wedge - a composite implying 2 per cent growth against an actual 0.8 per cent - resolves toward the hard data more often than not. By the second quarter of 2027 the Reserve Bank will be looking at a 2 per cent CPI forecast and a labour market with a five-and-a-half handle, and the hiking cycle will be shorter than September's track implies. tactical.analysis: The global risk backdrop is close to as good as it gets and the New Zealand dollar has conspicuously failed to monetise it, which is why this factor generates no tactical signal despite an obviously supportive environment. The VIX closed at 14.43 on 28 August against 20.66 a month earlier, a 6.23 point collapse; the S&P 500 finished August at 7,686.14 near its highs; United States investment-grade option-adjusted spreads are 79 basis points and high-yield 263 basis points, both near cycle tights and both tighter than a month ago when high yield stood at 287. The New Zealand dollar is the highest-beta risk-on currency in the G10 - lower liquidity than the Australian dollar, no Federal Reserve swap line, and a documented tendency to gap and overshoot in stress - so in a regime like this it should be leading the pack. Instead NZD/USD is up 0.48 per cent over one month and down 1.04 per cent over twelve, while the broad dollar index itself fell 2.04 points in August. The one place the risk beta has expressed itself is NZD/JPY, the purest risk barometer in G10 foreign exchange, which is up 7.49 per cent over twelve months and sits at the 91st percentile of its 52-week range - but that is a carry story running through the 150 basis point differential to the Bank of Japan, not a risk story. The correlation structure described in the currency brief, with NZD/USD running plus 0.85 to plus 0.95 to AUD/USD and minus 0.3 to minus 0.5 to the VIX, has not broken down so much as been overwhelmed by the relative-rates axis. Tail risks over the next four weeks are identifiable and two-sided: a Federal Reserve hike on 16 September, Chinese manufacturing at 49.8 on the official measure, a second month below 50 but improving from 49.2, and reported United States-Iran fighting driving oil. The honest tactical read is that a supportive regime is already fully banked with no cushion left if volatility normalises.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months a VIX of 14.43 and a high-yield spread of 263 basis points are levels to fade rather than extrapolate, and the New Zealand dollar has the worst convexity in the G10 to that fade. The currency brief is explicit about the mechanism: New Zealand is more vulnerable to risk-off drawdowns than Australia because of lower liquidity, positions are harder to exit in stress, and the Reserve Bank has no standing United States dollar swap line with the Federal Reserve where the Reserve Bank of Australia does. Layer onto that a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP that requires continuous foreign capital inflow and a net international investment position of minus 42.8 per cent of GDP, and the New Zealand dollar is structurally short global risk appetite in a way that does not show up in a benign environment and shows up violently in a hostile one. The specific channels of deterioration over the horizon are identifiable. China, New Zealand's largest export destination, printed second-quarter GDP of 4.3 per cent below its own 4.5 to 5 per cent target, and its official manufacturing PMI was 49.8 in August - a second month below 50, but a rebound from 49.2 and better than the 49.7 consensus, and the S&P Global RatingDog measure actually rose to 51.5. Chinese dairy buying was nonetheless described as being at historic lows at the June auction and July whole milk powder exports to China down 12.8 per cent year on year. The Federal Reserve is priced for a hike rather than a cut, which is the classic configuration for a risk-off dollar rally that hits high-beta currencies twice, through both the risk and the funding channel. And the correlation the brief expects - New Zealand dollar following the Australian dollar with amplification - has been running one way for a year, with AUD/NZD up 8.72 per cent, meaning the New Zealand dollar has been the shock absorber for the pair rather than the beneficiary. A benign regime that has already delivered nothing to this currency is not a strategic support.

strategic.what_is_priced: Credit and volatility markets price a continuation of the current regime for the full strategic horizon, with no premium for a Chinese demand shock or a hawkish Federal Reserve surprise. We think both risks are underpriced and that the New Zealand dollar is the G10 currency least able to absorb either. The strategic edge here is not a forecast of higher volatility but the observation that this currency retains all of the downside beta while having demonstrably forfeited the upside.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The split is a function of where a risk indicator sits in its distribution rather than any change in the New Zealand dollar itself. Over two to four weeks a VIX of 14.43 and a high-yield spread of 263 basis points are simply the prevailing conditions, and since the currency has already declined to respond to them they generate no directional information - hence Neutral. Over one to six months those same levels are extremes from which the distribution of outcomes is heavily skewed toward deterioration, and the New Zealand dollar's structural characteristics - lowest G10 liquidity, no Federal Reserve swap line, a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP external deficit requiring continuous funding - convert that skew into a directional negative.

tactical.analysis: The Commitments of Traders report for 25 August, released on 28 August and the most recent print available at the valuation date, shows leveraged funds net short 31,994 New Zealand dollar contracts - 3,673 long against 35,667 short - having added 5,188 contracts to that short over the week, while asset managers covered 20,823 shorts to swing 25,889 contracts and finish net long 430. Total open interest is 88,964 contracts of 100,000 New Zealand dollars each, which makes this one of the two smallest currency futures markets in the G10 and means small absolute changes represent large percentage shifts. The currency brief sets the notable threshold for this market at plus or minus 30,000 contracts, so the leveraged short is marginally past the level at which squeezes historically become disorderly, and it is running into a Monetary Policy Statement where the decision is 94 per cent priced but the OCR track is a genuine unknown. That is the classic asymmetric setup: the event cannot disappoint the shorts on the rate, only on the track, and the track has only one direction available to it given the Reserve Bank hiked off-cycle in July. The divergence between the two trader categories reinforces the read, because real money stepping out of a short a week before the event is more often a leading indicator than a coincidence. The reason confidence sits at 50 rather than higher is a genuine and unresolved data conflict: the legacy non-commercial series carried in the pipeline calendar shows minus 14,200 contracts for the same report date and a large positive weekly swing, disagreeing with the Traders in Financial Futures series on both level and direction, most likely because one is futures-only and the other futures-and-options on a different trader taxonomy. We use the primary CFTC figures, disclose the conflict, and refuse to build a high-conviction squeeze case on a number we cannot reconcile. The corroborating instrument that would normally settle it - 25-delta risk reversals, which the currency brief identifies as a better proxy than CFTC data for this market - is not obtainable from any free source.

tactical.what_is_priced: With leveraged funds short 31,994 contracts and adding, the market is positioned for the Reserve Bank to deliver the priced hike and stop there. The track is the variable that positioning is not hedged for, and a published terminal near 3.5 per cent would force covering into a resistance band starting at 0.59505. strategic.analysis: Positioning carries almost no information at a one-to-six-month horizon in this market and the honest stance is Neutral at low confidence. Speculative futures positions in the New Zealand dollar turn over in weeks: the asset-manager book swung 25,889 contracts in a single week, which is 29 per cent of total open interest, so whatever the book looks like today tells you nothing about February. The structural point that does survive the horizon is the size of the market rather than its direction - 88,964 contracts of total open interest is roughly two per cent of what the euro carries, so the New Zealand dollar has no positioning shock absorber and any sustained directional flow moves spot rather than open interest. The currency brief notes that Japanese retail investors through margin foreign exchange platforms are significant New Zealand dollar carry holders, and that channel is not visible in CFTC data at all; it matters strategically because the 150 basis point carry against the yen that supports it is the leg with the most identifiable reversal risk if the Bank of Japan normalises further from 1.00 per cent against core inflation of 1.8 per cent. There are no meaningful New Zealand dollar exchange-traded funds to read flows from, no sovereign wealth or reserve manager activity of consequence given the currency's roughly two per cent share of global turnover, and no obtainable option skew. What can be said is that the current leveraged short of 31,994 contracts is not an extreme by historical standards for this market - the prior dossier recorded minus 47,700 contracts on the 31 July legacy basis - so there is neither a stretched short to squeeze nor a crowded long to unwind over the strategic horizon. Positioning is genuinely neutral information here, which is the correct conclusion rather than a failure to form one.

The only strategically meaningful positioning fact is the unmeasured Japanese retail carry book in NZD/JPY, which is priced as though the Bank of Japan will hold at 1.00 per cent indefinitely - an assumption Japanese core inflation of 1.8 per cent does not obviously support.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: Positioning is one of the few factors where the same data legitimately produces different stances across horizons, because its half-life is shorter than the strategic window. Tactically a 31,994 contract leveraged short running into a Monetary Policy Statement with an unpriced OCR track is a directional signal with a defined catalyst two to four weeks out. Strategically the same book turns over roughly every four to six weeks - the asset-manager category alone moved 29 per cent of total open interest in one week - so it contains no information about where the currency sits in February, and the stance reverts to Neutral.
factors.contrarian_analysis_tactical: Positioning is moderately stretched but not extreme. The currency brief sets the notable threshold at plus or minus 30,000 contracts because New Zealand dollar open interest is one of the smallest in the G10, and leveraged funds at minus 31,994 sit just past it - stretched enough that a squeeze would be disorderly, not so stretched that it must happen. The unwind trigger is specific and dated: an OCR track published on 2 September pointing at a terminal near 3.5 per cent rather than the 3.3 per cent of the May track, against market pricing of roughly one further move after September. A squeeze from here would be violent in pip terms because the first resistance band at 0.59505 to 0.5997 sits only 58 pips above spot and the heavy 0.6022 to 0.6072 band with six touches is the next stop, so 100 to 150 pips of covering could happen inside two sessions in a market with 88,964 contracts of open interest and an ATR14 of 42 pips. The other side of the trade sees a central bank hiking into 5.6 per cent unemployment, falling real wages, house prices 17 per cent below peak and a 185 basis point deficit to Australia, and concludes that whatever the Reserve Bank publishes it will not be delivered - which is exactly what the two-year at roughly 121 basis points through Australia already says. Both sides are coherent; the short side is better funded and worse timed.
factors.contrarian_analysis_strategic: Over one to six months the contrarian case inverts. If the September track is hawkish and the shorts do cover, the New Zealand dollar will enter the fourth quarter with a cleaner positioning slate at exactly the moment the fundamental case deteriorates - the fuel base effect reversing out of the CPI, terms of trade falling for a second consecutive quarter, Fonterra's forecast already cut from 9.75 to 9.25 New Zealand dollars per kilogram of milk solids, and a general election plus a Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update on 29 September in front of two rating agencies already on negative outlook. A covered short base removes the mechanical support that has been quietly limiting downside all year. The historical analogue is instructive: the prior dossier recorded a legacy net short of 47,700 contracts on 31 July, roughly a third larger than today, and the currency still only managed plus 0.48 per cent over the following month - a short base that large failing to produce a rally is evidence that the selling is fundamental rather than speculative. The strategic contrarian risk to our own bearish view is a Bank of Japan hold combined with a 3.5 per cent New Zealand terminal rate, which would rebuild the Japanese retail carry book in NZD/JPY and support the currency through a channel no positioning report captures.

tactical.analysis: The tactical external picture is dominated by a single ugly print and a dairy recovery that is real but shallow. New Zealand's July merchandise trade balance came in at minus 1.95 billion New Zealand dollars against a market expectation nearer minus 175 million, with exports of 7.39 billion and imports of 9.34 billion, and the annual balance deteriorated from minus 3.75 billion to minus 5.24 billion in a single month - a 1.49 billion swing. Against that, GlobalDairyTrade has now printed four consecutive positive auctions after the 4.9 per cent collapse on 7 July: plus 1.5 per cent on 21 July, plus 0.1 per cent on 4 August, plus 2.3 per cent on 18 August and plus 0.9 per cent at Event 411 on 1 September, the valuation date itself, with an average winning price of 3,910 United States dollars per tonne across 157 bidders. But whole milk powder, the reference product that actually drives the Fonterra payout, was down 0.1 per cent at 3,585 dollars and remains below its 3,706 dollar level of early June, and cheddar fell 6.6 per cent at the September event. The ANZ World Commodity Price Index fell 3.9 per cent in July in world terms and 4.0 per cent in New Zealand dollar terms, the largest monthly decline since November 2022, with the dairy sub-index down 6.5 per cent on the month and 11.3 per cent on the year and aluminium down 8.2 per cent. Two dated events land inside the tactical window and both skew negative: the ANZ commodity index for August on 3 September and the June-quarter Overseas Trade Indexes on 3 September - note that this is 3 September, not 2 September as the cached calendar states - following a March-quarter terms of trade decline of 2.0 per cent driven by export prices falling 2.7 per cent against import prices falling only 0.7 per cent. Dairy has stopped falling; it has not started paying.

That is a small, dated, tactical negative sitting directly inside the same week as the Monetary Policy Statement.

strategic.analysis: This is the dominant strategic factor at a 0.16 weight and it is clearly negative. New Zealand's current account deficit of 16.3 billion New Zealand dollars, or 3.6 per cent of GDP, for the year to March 2026 has narrowed from 4.2 per cent a year earlier, but the improvement stalled three quarters ago - the annual figure has gone from minus 16.28 billion in June 2025 to minus 15.36, minus 16.00 and back to minus 16.30 - and the composition is the problem. The goods deficit widened 323 million in the March quarter, the services surplus was a bare 33 million, and the primary income deficit was minus 3.3 billion, which is structural: New Zealand pays a large and non-cyclical income stream to foreign owners of its net liabilities, and the net international investment position of minus 193.1 billion, or minus 42.8 per cent of GDP, with net external debt at 49.0 per cent, is what generates it. Terms of trade fell 2.0 per cent in the March quarter and the June quarter print due 3 September is expected lower again. The commodity backdrop is deteriorating on trend rather than on noise: the ANZ dairy sub-index is down 11.3 per cent year on year, Fonterra cut its 2026/27 farmgate forecast from a 9.75 dollar midpoint to 9.25 on 13 July, explicitly because GDT reference-product prices had fallen 11 per cent since the opening forecast on strong global supply, and whole milk powder at 3,585 dollars is going sideways at a level that does not support the old forecast. The demand side is worse. China, New Zealand's largest export destination and the buyer of most of its dairy, printed second-quarter GDP of 4.3 per cent below its own target and an official manufacturing PMI of 49.8 in August, a second month below 50 though improving from 49.2 and beating a 49.7 consensus; Chinese buying at the June auction was described as being at historic lows; July whole milk powder exports to China fell 12.8 per cent year on year; and infant formula demand is structurally impaired by a declining birth rate. Tourism is the one genuine offset, with travel services exports of 7.0 billion in the March quarter, up 1.3 billion year on year, but it is not large enough to close a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP gap. A country with dairy at roughly 30 per cent of merchandise exports, a single dominant customer whose manufacturing sector has spent two months just below 50 while growing under its own GDP target, and a structural income deficit does not get a currency tailwind from its external accounts over six months. Staleness and sourcing flags added after adversarial verification: the balance of payments figures are for the March 2026 quarter, roughly 154 days past the reference-period end and well outside the 60-day strategic window, with the June-quarter release not due until 16 September. In addition, Statistics New Zealand release pages are JavaScript-gated in this stack and return empty bodies, so the headline figures were confirmed from page metadata while the external-sector detail - the current account ratio, the net international investment position, net external debt and the monthly trade balances - is best available and flagged rather than read from the cited page body.

It is not pricing the stall in that improvement over the last three quarters, the 11.3 per cent year-on-year decline in dairy prices, the Fonterra downgrade, or a Chinese manufacturing sector that has spent two months below 50 on the official measure - though we note, and have lowered confidence for, the fact that the August reading improved from 49.2 and beat consensus while the S&P Global RatingDog measure rose to 51.5. We expect the terms of trade to fall for a second consecutive quarter and the current account to stop improving, which is worth more to the currency over six months than any plausible policy convergence.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The stance is Bearish at both horizons but confidence rises from 58 to 62 as the weight rises from 0.06 to 0.16, because the tactical evidence is two scheduled releases and one bad trade print while the strategic evidence is a structural income deficit, a 30 per cent export concentration in a commodity whose price is down 11.3 per cent year on year, and a dominant customer whose manufacturing sector has run below 50 for two months. Tactically the four-auction dairy recovery genuinely offsets some of the damage and caps confidence; strategically the recovery is 0.9 per cent on an index whose reference product is still below its June level, which offsets nothing. The mechanism is simply that balance-of-payments flows accumulate, and six months of a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP deficit funded from abroad is a real constraint where four weeks of it is not.

tactical.analysis: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is the only G10 central bank that publishes its own projected policy path, which makes the gap between that path and market pricing the cleanest guidance signal in the developed world - and on 2 September it republishes that path for the first time since May. The July Record of Meeting is unambiguous in tone: the Committee said that some further reduction in monetary stimulus is likely to be required to return inflation to the 2 per cent target midpoint, that while further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings their timing is highly uncertain, that increasing the OCR was intended in part to avoid an unwarranted further easing in financial conditions, and - most tellingly - that the current level of the OCR remains accommodative at 2.50 per cent. It also warned that if sustained, a lower exchange rate could add to medium-term inflation pressures, which is an explicit statement that the Bank will lean against currency weakness. The July decision was reached by consensus with no dissent, a marked consolidation from the 3-3 split of 27 May that had to be resolved by the chair's casting vote, and the disclosed risk assessment showed Gai and Gourley judging risks skewed to the upside against Breman, Conway, Hansen and Silk seeing them as broadly balanced. Governor Anna Breman therefore arrives at her September statement with a unanimous committee, an inflation print of 4.1 per cent and a track that is four months old and already superseded by events. Market pricing implies roughly one further move beyond September, while Westpac expects the track to imply 3.0 per cent by year-end with a terminal near 3.28 per cent and BNZ expects a published peak around 3.5 per cent. That is a 25 to 50 basis point hawkish gap between guidance and pricing, and the Bank has both the mandate and the recent behaviour to close it in its own favour. Flag added after adversarial verification: the May 2026 Monetary Policy Statement publishes its OCR track as a chart rather than a numeric table on the web version, so the quarterly track values and the approximately 3.3 per cent terminal quoted throughout this report are best available and flagged. The terminal is corroborated only indirectly, by Westpac's 3.28 per cent unrounded figure in its September preview, and the MPS text itself gives scenario OCR peaks of 4.3 and 3.6 per cent rather than a stated central-track terminal. Confidence on this factor has been reduced accordingly.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices roughly one 25 basis point move beyond September, implying a terminal near 3.00 to 3.25 per cent, while the Bank's own superseded track already reaches 3.1 per cent by mid-2027 and the two most credible local previews expect a published path at or above 3.28 per cent. The gap between guidance and pricing is therefore 25 to 50 basis points and it points in the hawkish direction. This is the single most tradable guidance mispricing in the G10 right now precisely because the Reserve Bank is the only central bank that will resolve it with a published number.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the published track stops being a signal and starts being a test, and the Reserve Bank's recent record does not inspire confidence that it will pass. The May 2026 track had the OCR at a 2.5 per cent quarterly average for the September 2026 quarter - a level reached only because the Bank hiked off that track in July - and had CPI peaking at 4.3 per cent in the September quarter, a figure the July Monetary Policy Review had to revise down to 3.3 per cent within eight weeks. A track that needs revising twice in a quarter is a weaker instrument than its reputation suggests. The deeper strategic problem is that whatever the Bank publishes on 2 September will be conditioned on the inflation it can see, and the inflation it can see is a fuel shock: tradables at 4.9 per cent against a sectoral factor model pinned at 2.7 per cent for four quarters, with Brent already 12 per cent off its July high. The Bank's own forecast has CPI at 2.4 per cent by mid-2027 and 2.0 per cent by September 2027, which means the Bank is publishing a rising OCR path alongside a CPI path that returns to target - a combination that is internally coherent only if it believes the domestic economy is stronger than unemployment at a decade-high 5.6 per cent, real wages falling 2.1 per cent and retail volumes turning negative suggest. The public appears not to believe it either, with one-year inflation expectations down 81 basis points to 2.60 per cent. The credibility question is therefore two-sided and genuinely balanced: the Reserve Bank is among the most transparent central banks in the G10 and has just demonstrated willingness to act, which is credibility-positive, but the instrument it uses is a conditional forecast that has already been wrong twice this year in the direction that matters. Neutral at 48 is a considered conclusion here, not a default: the hawkish September signal and the high probability of a subsequent dovish revision offset almost exactly over the strategic window. strategic.what_is_priced: The market treats the RBNZ track as informative but discountable, pricing a terminal roughly 25 basis points below where the Bank is likely to publish one. Over six months we think the market is right and the Bank is wrong, because the Bank's own CPI forecast returns to target while its OCR path rises. The strategic edge is not in fading the September track immediately but in expecting the December track to be revised down, which is when the guidance factor flips from a New Zealand dollar support to a New Zealand dollar drag.

factors.horizon_split_explanation: The split is mechanical and turns on the publication calendar. Tactically there is one track, it lands on 2 September, it is four months stale, and every credible preview points to it moving up - so guidance is a New Zealand dollar positive with a dated catalyst. Strategically there are two tracks inside the window, the second on 9 December, and the conditions that would force the December revision - a fuel base effect reversing out of tradables inflation, unemployment above 5.6 per cent and one-year expectations already at 2.60 per cent - are visible now. Guidance supports the currency for a month and then becomes the instrument through which the disinflation is transmitted to the front end.

tactical.analysis: The four weeks in front of the valuation date are unusually dense with scheduled events and unusually free of binary political ones, which is why the tactical stance is Neutral rather than directional. The dominant event is the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Statement on 2 September, but at 94 per cent priced for a 25 basis point hike the decision cannot generate a surprise on the rate - only the published OCR track can, and that risk is captured in Factors 1 and 6 rather than here. The terms of trade for the June quarter and the ANZ commodity index for August both land on 3 September, second-quarter GDP on 17 September, the balance of payments on 16 September, and GlobalDairyTrade Event 412 in the middle of the month on its fortnightly cadence. The largest genuinely two-sided event is external: the Federal Open Market Committee on 16 September, which carries a Summary of Economic Projections and where the market prices a sourced 26 to 60 per cent probability of a hike against no more than 5 per cent for a cut - an unusually wide and unusually hawkish distribution that would hit the New Zealand dollar through both the risk and the funding channels. The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update on 29 September sits at the edge of the tactical window and is the first genuinely political event of the cycle. Geopolitically, reported United States-Iran fighting has been moving Brent, which cuts both ways for New Zealand: higher oil sustains the tradables inflation that justifies the hikes but worsens the terms of trade for a net energy importer. Options are pricing almost none of this - the volatility term structure is in orderly contango at 7.885, 8.183 and 8.365 per cent across 43.6, 99.6 and 190.6 days, with no near-dated event premium at all.

tactical.what_is_priced: The options market is charging essentially nothing for event risk, with the term structure in contango into a Monetary Policy Statement, an FOMC with projections and a quarterly GDP print inside sixteen days. That is a mispricing of the distribution rather than of the direction: we do not have a strong view on which way the events resolve, but we are confident the market is underpaying for the possibility that they resolve loudly. Directional conviction and optionality are both cheap here.

strategic.analysis: The strategic event calendar is materially more hostile than the tactical one because it contains New Zealand's three-year political cycle. A general election is expected in November 2026 - the exact polling day was not confirmed in the sources consulted and is not asserted here - preceded by a Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update on 29 September that will publish an independent Treasury view of the fiscal accounts into a campaign. New Zealand's political parties differ materially on housing, immigration and fiscal policy, and all three transmit directly to the currency: immigration settings drive the net migration flows that a country of 5.3 million cannot absorb smoothly, housing policy drives the dominant channel of the domestic economy, and fiscal policy meets two of three rating agencies already sitting on negative outlook. That combination - an election, a fiscal update, and Moody's and Fitch both on negative watch - is the kind of cluster that produces a headline risk premium in a small, illiquid currency without any single event needing to go badly. The second strategic exposure is China, which is both New Zealand's largest export destination and the source of most of its dairy demand, and where second-quarter GDP of 4.3 per cent undershot the official target while August manufacturing was 49.8 on the official measure, a second month below 50 though improving from 49.2 and beating consensus. Any disruption to the China-New Zealand dairy relationship, whether through tariffs, market access or simply weaker infant formula demand from a declining birth rate, is the single largest identifiable tail for this currency and the currency brief names it as such. Third, GlobalDairyTrade auctions run fortnightly, which is the highest-frequency commodity event affecting any G10 currency, and a fall greater than 5 per cent at any one of them moves the New Zealand dollar intraday - there will be roughly twelve of them inside the strategic horizon. Fourth, New Zealand is earthquake-prone and the currency brief notes the historical pattern of an initial weakening on damage. None of these is individually likely; collectively they skew the distribution.

A Pre-election Update published into a campaign, by an independent Treasury, against forecasts that were set in May, is the natural venue for that trajectory to be marked to market - and a campaign is the natural venue for both major parties to add to it. tactical.analysis: The single most consequential fact for a non-dollar currency right now is that the Federal Reserve is priced for a hike rather than a cut, and the New Zealand dollar is the G10 currency least equipped to absorb one. The market prices a sourced 26 to 60 per cent probability of a 25 basis point increase at the 16 September meeting and no more than 5 per cent for a cut, with the target range at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent, effective fed funds at 3.63 per cent and a Taylor-rule implied rate of 4.71 per cent; the range rather than a point estimate is stated because CME FedWatch is not obtainable from a citable URL in this stack, and the range is flagged. Funding conditions themselves are calm: the Secured Overnight Financing Rate printed 3.68 per cent on 31 August against 3.65 on 28 August, comfortably inside the target range with no dislocation, and no swap line usage has been reported. Quantitative tightening is still running - the Federal Reserve balance sheet fell to 6.7309 trillion dollars on 26 August from 6.7457 trillion on 19 August and 6.7600 trillion on 12 August, a pace of roughly 15 billion dollars a week - so dollar reserves are still being drained at the margin even as the price of dollars is stable. The specific New Zealand dollar funding measure is derivable rather than quoted: the futures-implied roll premium of plus 91.0 basis points annualised, approximately corroborated by a six-month forward premium of 26.76 points equal to plus 90.9 basis points - a re-read of the same live quote screen 35 minutes later gave plus 95.6 basis points, so the agreement is within about five basis points rather than exact, and is flagged - sits against a policy differential of minus 112.5 basis points and against SOFR versus the OCR of minus 118, which implies a cross-currency basis of roughly minus 21 to minus 27 basis points. That is a modest dollar funding premium and not a stress signal - but it is a premium, and the currency brief is explicit that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, unlike the Reserve Bank of Australia, has no standing dollar swap line with the Federal Reserve. A country running a 3.6 per cent-of-GDP current account deficit into a tightening dollar with no swap line is structurally exposed.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the dollar liquidity channel is a persistent headwind for the New Zealand dollar for three separable reasons. First, the direction of United States policy: with the target range at 3.50 to 3.75 per cent, effective fed funds at 3.63 per cent, a Taylor-rule implied 4.71 per cent and Chair Warsh having said the Federal Reserve still has work to do, the distribution of United States policy outcomes over the horizon is skewed toward tighter. That directly compounds the New Zealand dollar's minus 112.5 basis point carry deficit, and even on our own constructive Reserve Bank path - two more hikes to 3.00 per cent - a single Federal Reserve hike leaves the deficit at 87 basis points. Second, the quantity channel: quantitative tightening is still draining reserves at roughly 15 billion dollars a week from a 6.7309 trillion dollar balance sheet, and while there is no evidence yet of reserve scarcity, the direction of travel over six months is toward less abundant dollar liquidity rather than more. Third, and specific to this currency, New Zealand must import capital continuously to fund a current account deficit of 3.6 per cent of GDP against a net international investment position of minus 42.8 per cent and net external debt of 49.0 per cent, and it does so without a Federal Reserve swap line. The currency brief describes the dollar smile precisely for this case: the New Zealand dollar behaves like the Australian dollar with amplification, weakest at both ends and strongest in the goldilocks middle, and more vulnerable than the Australian dollar at the extremes because of lower liquidity and the absent swap line. The dollar is currently in the benign middle - the broad index fell 2.04 points in August - which is the best the New Zealand dollar can hope for, and it has still produced minus 1.04 per cent over twelve months. The derived cross-currency basis of minus 21 to minus 27 basis points is comfortable today and is worth monitoring precisely because it is the instrument that would move first if the funding environment turned. Note that the derivation cannot be made exact without an OIS curve.

tactical.rationale: At tactical weights the dossier is a rates story with a funding brake. Policy and Rates at 0.24 and Inflation and Growth at 0.18 together carry 42 per cent of the weight and both are Bullish, because the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is one of only two G10 central banks in an active tightening cycle and because a 4.1 per cent headline CPI print gives it no choice about 2 September. The weighted score of plus 0.2230 is a modest positive and it maps to conviction 3, which is the honest reading: this is a view worth having, not a view worth pressing. The factors reinforce each other cleanly on the hawkish side - a 4.1 per cent CPI print forces the hike, the hike forces a republished OCR track, the track lands on a leveraged-fund short of 31,994 contracts, and the currency brief tells us this is one of the two smallest currency futures markets in the G10 - which is a coherent chain from data to policy to positioning to price. Actionability is good but not excellent - realised volatility at the 23rd percentile of its year and a term structure in contango mean a directional view is cheap to own through options, while the 74-pip base case against a 72-pip downside means spot expression offers almost no edge at all. The three things that would change this quickly are a track that merely ratifies May, a Federal Reserve hike on 16 September, and a June-quarter terms of trade print worse than the minus 2.0 per cent of March.

cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The divergence is driven by the weight schedule far more than by any change in the underlying data, and the arithmetic makes it explicit. External Balance and Terms of Trade nearly triples from 0.06 to 0.16 while Inflation and Growth falls from 0.18 to 0.10, so the factor carrying the bearish case gains 10 points of weight and the factor carrying the bullish case loses 8. Three factors also change stance across horizons for substantive reasons: Inflation and Growth flips from Bullish to Bearish because the 4.1 per cent headline that forces the September hike rests on a petrol base effect that reverses inside the strategic window; Guidance and Credibility falls from Bullish to Neutral because the September track that supports the currency for a month becomes the instrument through which a December downgrade is transmitted; and Flows falls from Bullish to Neutral because a futures book that turns over 29 per cent of open interest in a single week carries no six-month information.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The second half of October 2026. Specifically the September-quarter CPI release in the third week of October, which is the first print in which the petrol base effect substantially unwinds and where a headline materially below 4.1 per cent removes the justification for the tightening cycle, followed by the 28 October Monetary Policy Review at which the Reserve Bank has its first opportunity to soften the September framing.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: The September-quarter CPI printing at or below 3.5 per cent while the sectoral factor model stays at or below 2.7 per cent. That single combination converts the inflation factor from a policy accelerant into a disinflation confirmation, and it is what turns a hawkish track published on 2 September into a track that has to be revised on 9 December.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Express the tactical view through options rather than spot and let it expire rather than rolling it. seasonality.pattern: Two patterns are relevant and both are commodity rather than currency conventions. First, the New Zealand dairy production season runs from June to May with peak milk flows through September to November, which mechanically increases GlobalDairyTrade offer volumes in the spring and has historically weighed on auction clearing prices during exactly that window. Event 411 on 1 September offered a maximum of 46,146 tonnes against a minimum of 39,005, with 43,976 tonnes sold. Second, the general G10 pattern of year-end portfolio rebalancing and reduced liquidity in December applies with above-average force to the New Zealand dollar because it is the least liquid major currency and the currency brief warns explicitly that positions are harder to exit and the pair gaps in thin markets.
seasonality.relevance_window: Both patterns fall inside the strategic horizon. The dairy supply peak covers September to November 2026, overlapping the four GDT auctions most likely to test whether the current four-auction recovery is genuine. The December liquidity effect covers the final month of the horizon and coincides with the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement and the 9 December FOMC.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Not quantified here. No dated, citable measurement of the seasonal amplitude in either the GDT index or New Zealand dollar December liquidity was obtained from a primary source, and no figure is asserted. The patterns are noted as directional context only.
seasonality.current_alignment: Aligned with the strategic bearish view but not load-bearing for it. The spring supply peak arrives with whole milk powder already at 3,585 US dollars per tonne, below its 2 June level of 3,706, and with Fonterra having cut its 2026/27 forecast midpoint from 9.75 to 9.25 New Zealand dollars on exactly the grounds of strong global supply. The December liquidity effect amplifies whatever direction is in force rather than creating one.

assumptions: The gated pipeline cache is treated as authoritative wherever it carries a precise current number - policy rates, spot and cross levels, realised volatility, moving averages, support and resistance zones, BIS real effective exchange rates, the futures-implied roll premium and the central-bank meeting calendar - and research supplies context, narrative and citations around those figures rather than replacing them. Where the store tail of 0.59164 as at 31 August sits above the RBNZ 2pm fix of 0.59135 on 1 September and the TradingEconomics New York close of 0.5894, the store value is retained because the downstream pair analysis uses it, and the roughly 3 to 22 pip gap is disclosed rather than presented as a corroborated vendor close.

The valuation date is 2026-09-01 and the information cutoff is treated as end of day on that date. The RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement of 2 September 2026 is therefore analysed as the dominant forthcoming catalyst and its outcome is not assumed or reported. Where a figure was necessarily read on 2 September - the FXEmpire forward points at 01:52 UTC, and a live TradingEconomics US 10-year quote - this is stated explicitly at the point of use.

The purchasing-power-parity table is a REER-relative proxy and is explicitly NOT a purchasing-power-parity fair-value estimate. Deviations are computed as the ratio of New Zealand's BIS real effective exchange rate of 101.12 to each peer's, less one, and converted to an implied level at the prevailing spot. The BIS period is 2026-06, roughly 63 days before the valuation date and marginally outside the strategic freshness window. The JPY row in particular is an artefact of the yen's index base and is labelled uninformative rather than actionable.

The cross-currency basis of roughly minus 21 to minus 27 basis points is a derivation, not a quote. It is obtained by subtracting the policy differential of minus 112.5 basis points, and alternatively the SOFR-versus-OCR gap of minus 118 basis points, from the observed NZD/USD futures-implied roll premium of plus 91.0 basis points annualised. Covered interest parity makes the roll premium equal to the interest differential plus the basis, and the two cannot be separated exactly without an OIS curve. No quoted EUR/USD or USD/JPY three-month basis was obtainable and none is asserted.

Carry-to-volatility ratios are computed as annualised carry in basis points divided by the 60-day realised volatility read directly from Data-Cache/derived/{PAIR}.json, not estimated and not recomputed, and the basis is stated wherever a ratio appears. For NZD/USD only, an implied-volatility-based ratio is also given using the genuine CME at-the-money quote of 8.183 per cent. No cross volatility has been constructed from two US dollar legs, and NZD/SEK is recorded as a gap rather than derived because the vendor carries no series for it.

Sovereign 10-year yields from the cached IRLTLT01 series are MONTHLY as at 2026-06-01, 92 days before the valuation date, and therefore breach both the 30-day tactical and 60-day strategic freshness windows. They are used only for like-for-like monthly spread comparisons where both legs share the same period, and are superseded by live 1 September quotes for New Zealand and Australia. Sovereign ratings are best available and marked as such: no rating-agency URL is fetchable and all three actions are secondary-corroborated.

The implied-volatility percentile field in the JSON is a zero placeholder and must not be read as a market level, because no history of implied volatility is obtainable. The closest measurable analogue, stated separately, is that the 20-day realised volatility of 7.04 per cent sits at the 23rd percentile of its own trailing one-year distribution, derived in code from 261 daily observations of the gated weekday close series. Twenty-five-delta risk reversals and implied-volatility skew are not obtainable from any free source and no value is asserted anywhere in this report.

Positioning figures come from the CFTC Traders in Financial Futures report on a futures-only basis. They conflict with the legacy non-commercial series carried in the pipeline calendar, which shows minus 14,200 contracts for the same report date against minus 32,600 the prior week, disagreeing on both level and the direction of the weekly change. The probable cause is the futures-only versus futures-and-options basis and the different trader taxonomy. The primary CFTC figures are used, the conflict is disclosed, and positioning confidence is lowered to 50 tactically and 45 strategically as a result.

Bank forecasts have been corroborated individually at the publisher wherever possible rather than through aggregators. ANZ, Westpac New Zealand, BNZ, ING and MUFG are primary; UOB and Goldman Sachs were obtainable only through aggregators and are flagged as such; NAB's 0.63 is primary but dated 30 January 2026 and is excluded from the consensus cluster as stale. ASB, Kiwibank and HSBC levels were not obtainable and are documented gaps.

The Federal Reserve September hike probability is quoted as a range of 26 to 60 per cent rather than a point estimate because CME FedWatch is not obtainable from a citable URL in this stack and two independent prediction-market-derived reads disagreed materially. The width of the range is itself treated as information about how cleanly the event is priced.

Central-bank decision dates are taken exclusively from Data-Cache/calendar/central-bank-meetings.json and are never web-searched. Entries marked provisional in that file - notably the Bank of England's February 2027 date - are not presented as firm. Singapore is absent from that calendar by design because the Monetary Authority of Singapore operates an S$NEER policy band rather than a policy rate, and every Singapore cell in this report is research-sourced.

Where a peer's preferred core inflation measure was unavailable in the cached vintage store and could not be independently sourced - Australia, Canada, Switzerland and Sweden - the headline figure is repeated in the core column and labelled a documented gap rather than a measurement. Japanese CPI is absent from the cache entirely and the July 2026 rebasing to 2025 weights lowered measured inflation by roughly 0.2 percentage points, so Japanese year-on-year comparisons spanning July 2026 are vintage-inconsistent.

Adversarial verification was run against this dossier before shipping and returned 29 confirmed, 16 flagged and 8 unverifiable items. Its material findings have been applied: the four sovereign yield legs were corrected from an unreproducible vendor read of NZ 3.68/4.81 and AU 4.806/5.161 for 1 September to the RBNZ B2 official secondary-market closes of 3.61 and 4.74 for 31 August against Trading Economics Australian quotes of 4.82 and 5.195 for 2 September, which moves the load-bearing NZ-AU two-year spread from minus 112.6 to roughly minus 121 basis points and introduces a two-day basis mismatch that is flagged at every point of use; the MUFG forecast was corrected from 0.5800 for the fourth quarter of 2026 to 0.5900, with 0.5800 being the third quarter; the BNZ NZD/USD level could not be located at the publisher and BNZ has been removed from the consensus cluster; the BIS real effective exchange rate figures were confirmed to have no fetchable BIS source and are now labelled cache-sourced and flagged; the China manufacturing framing was corrected because the August official PMI of 49.8 was a rebound from 49.2 that beat a 49.7 consensus rather than a deterioration; and two GlobalDairyTrade dates in the signpost text were corrected from 23 and 8 July to 21 and 7 July. Every affected factor's confidence has been reduced and the weighted scores recomputed in code.

Two citations do not render in this stack and are flagged rather than removed. The ING G10 FX Talking article returns an empty body across repeated attempts, so the ING NZD/USD level of 0.60 is search-corroborated rather than read at the publisher. The CNBC China PMI URL returned HTTP 200 with an empty body, consistent with the standing cycle note, and has been replaced with the S&P Global RatingDog manufacturing PMI press release; the official NBS reading of 49.8 is corroborated across multiple secondary reports but has no fetchable primary URL in this stack and is marked best available. The FXEmpire forward page is a live quote screen whose values changed materially within 35 minutes of the original read, so the forward points are a snapshot that cannot be re-verified and the forward premium is stated as approximately 91 to 96 basis points annualised.
